Hmm, but folding the octagon in half gives a half-octagon; fold again gives quarter; third fold gives eighth; fourth fold gives sixteenth? But after 4 folds we get a triangle: the octagon has 8-fold symmetry; folding in half 3 times gives a 45° wedge (one-eighth), which is a triangle? Actually, one-eighth of the octagon (a wedge from center covering one edge) is a triangle with apex angle 45°. Folding 4 times: half (180° wedge), quarter (90° wedge), eighth (45° wedge), sixteenth (22.5° wedge) which is a right triangle half of the 45° wedge.

content:
Looking at the fold sequence, the final triangle has vertices at the octagon's center O, a vertex V, and an edge midpoint M (with the right angle at M). The cut removes the corner at the center O, perpendicular to the side OM (the fold line running to the edge midpoint).

- Because the cut is perpendicular to the fold line OM, each cut segment joins collinearly with its mirror image when unfolded across that fold.
- The 16 layers therefore produce 8 straight cut edges (instead of 16), forming an octagonal hole.
- Since the cut is perpendicular to the apothem fold (OM), the hole's edges are perpendicular to the same directions as the original octagon's edges — so the hole is an octagon oriented the same way as the outer octagon (vertices pointing the same directions), not rotated.

This matches the figure with the octagonal hole aligned with the outer octagon.

\boxed{B}
